one_liner: Block-independent LZ77 with zstd-coded token streams; decodes in parallel on CPU/GPU and supports random-access reads, aimed at genomic archives.
what_it_does: ACEAPEX is an LZ77 codec whose match search never leaves a 16 KiB block, so any block (and any byte range) can be decoded without the rest of the file; the tokens are split into four streams (literals, offsets, lengths, commands) that are entropy-coded in chunks with libzstd, or with its own rANS in the 'open' profile. It has its own ACEPX2 container (not a zstd frame), a C API (aceapex_compress/decompress/decompress_region/decompress_ranges, streaming encode and decode, a persistent region handle), a standalone C99 decoder, a Python reader and a CUDA decoder. It replaces zstd only where you control both ends and want parallel or ranged reads of write-once data.
how_it_is_fast: Confining matches to the block removes cross-block dependencies, so blocks decode in parallel across threads or GPU warps; inside a block the encoder redirects references to their earliest origin where it can verify the bytes, shortening dependency chains, and the GPU decoder resolves the rest by wavefront ordering and closed-form periodic fills. Entropy work is pushed into large zstd or AVX2 rANS chunks that decode independently of the match phase, and DNA literals get a 2-bit base packing with a case bitmask and exception list. Recent CPU gains come from literal tiles held in L2, transparent huge pages, and non-temporal output stores (CHANGELOG 2.3 draft).
when_to_use: Write-once, read-many archives of genomes (FASTA/FASTQ) where you need region reads by offset: the authors report 0.081 ms 16 KB seeks on chr1 against 0.140 ms for bgzip+fai, at 11.8% smaller size
Multi-core full decode of large files where you can spend 8 or more threads on decompression
GPU-resident data pipelines that decode compressed data on the device (open profile needs no nvCOMP)
Batched random range reads (aceapex_decompress_ranges) where requests cluster in the same blocks
when_not_to_use: As a general zstd replacement on one thread: independent lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P) shows aceapex 1.0.1 decoding silesia at about 675 MB/s against zstd -1 at 1351 MB/s, and the README's own single-thread FASTQ figure (1,624 MB/s) is below zstd -3's 2,026 MB/s
When interoperability matters: ACEPX2 is a private container, the lzbench copy is the older format 1, and archive bytes depend on the libzstd version used to encode
When ratio is the goal: the README says zstd -19 is 1.2-1.55x denser on FASTQ with a whole-file window
Write-heavy workloads: the README calls encode slow (50 GB at about 340 MB/s) and the project 'research-grade'
When you need a mature, long-fuzzed decoder for hostile input (see gotchas): the code changes daily and the 2.1.0 API returned wrong bytes under concurrent calls

integration.form: static lib or CLI from one C++ translation unit (src/aceapex_api.cpp); standalone C99 decoder as source-drop or shared lib (c/aceapex_decode.c); Python package; optional CUDA shared lib
integration.dependencies: libzstd (1.4.8 or 1.5.x; the open profile's archives need no zstd frames), pthreads; GPU Mode 2 needs NVIDIA nvCOMP 5 (closed source)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (g++ -O3 -march=native in the documented build), C99 for the decoder, nvcc with -std=c++17 for GPU (default target sm_75)
integration.platforms: x86-64, x86-32, ARM32, ARM64 and PPC64LE pass the release cross-matrix under qemu-user; MinGW builds the library but no Windows runner; CLI is POSIX (mmap); GPU on NVIDIA sm_75 and later (T4 to Blackwell tested)
integration.thread_safety: Per-call state since 2.2.0 (globals made thread-local after concurrent calls returned wrong bytes in 2.1.0; the lzbench 1.0.1 copy is unaffected); aceapex_decompress uses every hardware thread unless aceapex_decompress_mt is given a budget

gotchas: Possible integer overflow in header validation (from reading the code, not tested): both open_arc in c/aceapex_decode.c and ax_header_ok in src/aceapex_main.cpp check 68 + num_blocks*64 + zlit_sz + zoff_sz + zlen_sz + zcmd_sz <= src_size in unchecked uint64 arithmetic, so crafted 64-bit stream sizes can wrap the sum, pass the check and send stream pointers and cursor bounds outside the buffer in the in-memory API. The C decoder was fuzzed 2,400 runs and the C++ reader 3,000 runs under ASan/UBSan per the CHANGELOG, which random bytes would rarely hit.

The 'random access' unit is the entropy chunk, not the 16 KiB block: a region read unpacks the zstd or rANS chunks of all four streams that cover it (512 KiB default for token streams, 64 KiB to 1 MiB for literals), so seek cost and ratio depend on LIT_CHUNK and related knobs.

Tuning comes from environment variables (AX_PROFILE, ACEAPEX_BS, LIT_CHUNK and 13 more) only in builds with ACEAPEX_ENV_TUNING; the library inside lzbench, TurboBench or your program ignores them since 2.2.2, so CLI numbers may use settings your build does not.
nvCOMP 5.3.0.16 hangs on some corrupt zstd frames (repro in the repo); the GPU library offers ACEAPEX_GPU_VALIDATE_ZSTD to check every frame through libzstd on the host first.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over Zstandard or zlib-ng only when you need parallel or ranged decode of a large static file, especially genomic data or GPU-resident decode; Rapidgzip gives parallel decode while keeping the standard gzip format, and for plain single-thread speed LZ4, zstd and misa77 decode faster.
verified_claims_summary: The headline is first-party: on the 1 GB ERR194147 FASTQ (re-measured after an earlier sample with degenerate quality strings was withdrawn), 8-thread ACEAPEX decodes at 7,401 MB/s against zstd -3 at 2,026 MB/s at near-equal ratio (3.98 vs 3.96), where the zstd thread count is not stated and the CPU for that table is not named; single-thread ACEAPEX is 1,624 MB/s. The independent lzbench 2.4 table (EPYC 9555P, gcc 15.2.0, silesia, one thread) has the older 1.0.1 format at 675 MB/s decode, about half of zstd -1.
status_note: Very active (releases 2.1.0, 2.2.0 and 2.2.2 between 2026-09-29 and 2026-10-01, with a 2.3 draft open) and MIT-licensed with a written format spec and conformance fixtures, but self-described as research-grade; pin a release and validate untrusted archives before use.
